opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's a really natural thing to do and it creates a pretty systematic bias.

When people build a benchmark, there's a strong incentive to make it "hard." You want headroom, you don't want it saturated the day you release it. So the usual process is something like: you generate a big pool of candidate tasks, you run the current best models on them, and you keep the ones the models fail. That feels sensible, but what you've actually done is select on the residual. You've picked out exactly the tasks where current models happen to be weird or unlucky or have some idiosyncratic blind spot, relative to their general capability level.

And that has a couple of consequences. One is that when the next generation of models comes along, a lot of those tasks get solved really quickly. Partly the models have gotten better, but partly you're just seeing regression to the mean. The quirks that made one model fail aren't necessarily shared by the next one, so you get this apparent jump that overstates how much underlying progress happened. The flip side is that if you're measuring the models you filtered against, they look artificially terrible, close to zero, which makes the starting point look lower than it really is. So the slope you draw between them is distorted.

The other issue is that the tasks you end up with aren't representative of the thing you care about. If the question is "can this model do useful autonomous work in some domain," a set of tasks chosen because models fail at them is a strange, adversarially selected sample of that domain. Failures might come from ambiguous instructions, a broken environment, some obscure piece of knowledge, or a formatting gotcha, things that don't really reflect the capability you're trying to track. So the headline number tells you something more like "how good is the model at the weird corner cases we found" than "how capable is it."

That's a big part of why, in our work at METR, we've tried to build task suites in a way that doesn't condition on model performance, and to calibrate them against how long the tasks take skilled humans. If you have tasks that span a wide range of difficulty, from a few seconds to many hours of human time, and you didn't choose them based on whether models pass, you can say something meaningful about trends. You can look at something like the length of task a model completes with 50% reliability and see how that changes over time, and you're much less worried that the trend is an artifact of how you picked the questions.

There's also a forecasting angle. If benchmarks are built adversarially against the current frontier, you get this repeated pattern: a benchmark comes out, everyone says "look, models are still really bad at X," and then six months later it's mostly solved, and people get whiplash. That's bad for policymakers and anyone trying to plan, because the signal is noisy and biased in both directions depending on when you look. I'd much rather have measurements that are a bit less dramatic but give you a stable, interpretable trend line you can actually extrapolate from, with appropriate uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response discusses incentives to make benchmarks hard, but does not identify limited construction budgets as a constraint on task selection.

r002.rationale: It explains that filtering for current models’ failures selects idiosyncratic residuals, so later models may solve those tasks quickly through regression to the mean, creating an overstated apparent gain.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention labs creating benchmark-targeted synthetic training data as a cause of later gains.

r004.rationale: It favors task suites that do not condition on model performance and says this produces a more stable, interpretable trend line than weakness-selected benchmarks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a selection effect that's really easy to miss. When you're building a benchmark, the natural thing to do is to look for tasks that current models fail at, because those are the interesting ones, right? If the model already gets it right, it's not a very informative test. So you go hunting for failures, and you end up with a dataset that's enriched for whatever weird corners the current generation happens to be bad at.

The problem is that those corners aren't necessarily representative of the underlying capability you actually care about. Often what you've found is some idiosyncratic quirk of the training distribution, or a tokenization issue, or a particular kind of trick question that the model falls for. And then the next generation comes along and fixes that specific quirk, and the benchmark goes from, say, ten percent to ninety percent, and everyone says "wow, enormous progress." But the thing that changed might be pretty narrow. You've sort of measured the gap between the quirk and the fix, rather than measuring the broad capability.

And then the opposite distortion happens too. Because you filtered for things models were bad at, you've thrown away all the signal about what they were already good at. So the benchmark makes current models look worse than they are in some holistic sense, and then makes the improvement look more dramatic than it is. You get this sawtooth picture where everything looks hopeless until suddenly it's solved, and that's partly an artifact of how the tasks were chosen rather than a real discontinuity in capability.

What we've tried to do at METR is start from the other end. Instead of asking "what can't models do," ask "what do we actually want to know," which for us is something like, how long and how complex a task can an agent complete autonomously. Then you build a distribution of tasks that spans a range of difficulty, including things current models can do, and you track where on that distribution the frontier is. That way you're measuring something like a continuous quantity, and when the next model comes out you can see how far it moved along the axis, rather than just watching a number flip from "fail" to "pass."

It also matters for forecasting. If you want to predict when models will be able to do economically meaningful or dangerous things, you need a measure that has some stable meaning across generations. A benchmark that's defined by current failures doesn't have that property almost by construction, because the definition of the benchmark is anchored to one point in time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses filtering for tasks current models fail, but says nothing about limited benchmark-construction budgets constraining task selection.

r002.rationale: It says selected quirks can make later gains look dramatic, but attributes this to fixing narrow quirks; it does not identify regression to the mean as the mechanism.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention labs creating synthetic training data targeted at benchmark tasks.

r004.rationale: It contrasts selecting current-model failures with defining a task distribution around the capability of interest, spanning difficulty levels, and says this supports tracking a continuous frontier rather than a sawtooth pattern.

astra-6.text:
Well, if you choose tasks specifically because current models fail at them, you’re selecting on the thing you’re trying to measure. You can end up with a benchmark that makes systems look much less capable than they are across a representative set of tasks.

It can also distort the apparent trajectory. Suppose you collect all the tasks that today’s model can’t do, and then the next model solves a bunch of them. That might look like a sudden jump, even if the underlying improvement was fairly gradual—you’ve concentrated your measurement right around the previous model’s limits.

There’s nothing wrong with looking for failures. That’s useful for understanding limitations. But “a collection of things current models struggle with” and “a representative measure of capability” are different objects, and we should be clear about which one we’re using.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention benchmark-construction budgets constraining task selection.

r002.rationale: It says selecting tasks near a model’s limits can make later progress look sudden, but does not attribute unusually large gains to regression to the mean.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention labs creating synthetic training data targeted at the benchmarks.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes a representative task set from one selected for current weaknesses, but does not argue that defining the distribution from first principles produces steadier progress.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you choose tasks specifically because current models do badly on them, you’re selecting on the thing you’re trying to measure. You’ve deliberately excluded all the tasks where progress has already happened, so the resulting benchmark isn’t a representative sample of what we want AI systems to be able to do.

And then there’s a kind of moving-goalposts effect: once models get good at something, it stops being an interesting benchmark, and we find something else they can’t do. That can be useful for finding weaknesses, but if you interpret it as evidence about overall progress, you can end up with this picture where models are always failing, even as the set of things they can do keeps expanding. You need some stable task distribution, or at least an explicit account of how you selected the tasks, to make meaningful comparisons.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention low benchmark-construction budgets limiting task selection.

r002.rationale: It describes selection bias and moving goalposts, but does not explain unusually large subsequent gains as regression to the mean.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention labs creating benchmark-targeted synthetic training data.

r004.rationale: It recommends a stable task distribution for meaningful comparisons, but does not claim that defining one from first principles is more likely to produce a steady progress trend than selecting tasks for current weaknesses.
